variants.title: Walk the cache-aside read
variants.context: In cache-aside, the application reads Memcached first. A hit returns immediately. A miss makes the application read the authoritative source, store a disposable copy, and return the source result.
variants.prompt: A product page needs a product record. Put the read path in order.

items.text: On a miss, read the database, store a temporary copy, and return the source result.
Build a namespaced, versioned key and choose a short cache timeout.
Ask Memcached; a hit returns the bytes, a miss reports absence.
Hash the key to a server in the current pool.

variants.hint: The cache never loads the source itself; the application does.
variants.explanation: Key → server → get → source on miss. Memcached reports absence; it does not discover or load the value.

variants.title: Walk the cache-aside read
variants.context: In cache-aside, the application reads Memcached first. A hit returns immediately. A miss makes the application read the authoritative source, store a disposable copy, and return the source result.
variants.prompt: A request arrives just after the cache pool restarted. Put the read path in order.

items.text: Route the key to a server; the pool is empty but reachable.
Get returns a miss.
Read the source under admission control, then repopulate the cache.
Construct the key as usual.

variants.hint: A cold cache changes the outcome, not the order.
variants.explanation: The steps are identical; nearly every request follows the miss branch, so the source needs admission control during warm-up.

variants.title: Walk the cache-aside read
variants.context: In cache-aside, the application reads Memcached first. A hit returns immediately. A miss makes the application read the authoritative source, store a disposable copy, and return the source result.
variants.prompt: The cache lookup times out. Put the steps in order, including how the timeout is treated.

items.text: Route to the server and wait no longer than the timeout.
Fall back to the source with a concurrency limit and return its result.
Build the key with a bounded lookup timeout.
Record the timeout as its own telemetry, distinct from a miss.

variants.hint: Timeout, miss, and connection failure all fall back to the source but must be counted separately.
variants.explanation: A slow cache can make fallback slower than bypassing it. Bound the lookup, count the timeout, then take the source path.

variants.title: Read the memory signal
variants.context: Memcached assigns items to slab classes. Expiration marks a copy invalid; reclaim frees expired space lazily; eviction removes a live item when a class needs a chunk. An eviction is a capacity signal, not data loss.
variants.prompt: Evictions climb while total memory use is far below the limit. What is the most likely cause?
options: The server is dropping data it was told to keep.
The TTLs are long enough to fill the pool.
One slab class is under pressure while others hold idle pages.
optionFeedback: An eviction removes a disposable copy, and the source still has the data.
Long TTLs affect freshness; they do not create class imbalance.
Each size class behaves like its own small cache and can starve beside spare capacity.
variants.hint: Memory is allocated per size class, not as one pool.
variants.explanation: Inspect slab-class statistics. A pressured object-size band next to idle capacity is a distribution problem, not a total-RAM problem.

variants.title: Read the memory signal
variants.context: Memcached assigns items to slab classes. Expiration marks a copy invalid; reclaim frees expired space lazily; eviction removes a live item when a class needs a chunk. An eviction is a capacity signal, not data loss.
variants.prompt: A key’s TTL passed a minute ago, yet stats show its bytes are still counted. Is something broken?
options: No. Expired items are reclaimed lazily, not at the TTL.
Yes. Expiration must clear the bytes at the boundary.
Yes. The item was evicted and the stats are stale.
optionFeedback: The server does not synchronously clear every expired byte at the TTL boundary.
Expiration marks the copy invalid, and reclaim happens later on demand.
Eviction removes live items; an expired item is simply awaiting reclaim.
variants.hint: What does expiration guarantee, and what does it not?
variants.explanation: Expiration is a freshness boundary, not a durable deletion guarantee. Reads treat the item as gone even before its space is reclaimed.

variants.title: Read the memory signal
variants.context: Memcached assigns items to slab classes. Expiration marks a copy invalid; reclaim frees expired space lazily; eviction removes a live item when a class needs a chunk. An eviction is a capacity signal, not data loss.
variants.prompt: A team stores one 900 KB blob per page instead of several small objects. What is the main cost?
options: Serialization cost, allocator waste, and a wider blast radius.
Nothing, because fewer keys always means fewer round trips.
Memcached refuses to store any value larger than 1 KB.
optionFeedback: Giant values cost more on every path, and one miss rebuilds everything.
Fewer keys can mean far more bytes per request and a worse slab fit.
Large values are configurable, but their cost is the point.
variants.hint: What happens on a single miss of that key?
variants.explanation: Prefer compact, independently refreshable objects when readers do not always need the whole payload.

variants.title: Choose the invalidation rule
variants.context: Every cached value must be disposable. TTL suits bounded staleness; delete-after-commit races with refills; versioned keys retire old representations; CAS rejects a write when the item changed since it was read.
variants.prompt: The service deletes the cache key after each database commit, yet stale values keep appearing. What is the likely race?
options: The TTL is too short to cover the write window.
A refill that read the old row landed after the delete.
Delete is best-effort and can be dropped under load.
optionFeedback: A shorter or longer TTL bounds the damage but does not remove the race.
Delete-after-commit is simple, but a racing refill can put the old value back.
Delete is reliable here; the ordering of concurrent refills is the problem.
variants.hint: What was another caller doing while the write committed?
variants.explanation: Guard the refill: use CAS or versioned keys so an older refill cannot replace a newer value.

variants.title: Choose the invalidation rule
variants.context: Every cached value must be disposable. TTL suits bounded staleness; delete-after-commit races with refills; versioned keys retire old representations; CAS rejects a write when the item changed since it was read.
variants.prompt: A release changes the serialized shape of cached product records. How do you avoid a risky global flush?
options: Keep the same keys and hope the decoder copes.
Bump the representation version in the key.
Flush the whole pool at deploy time.
optionFeedback: Mixed representations under one key cause decode failures.
Versioned keys retire old representations without a flush storm.
A global flush turns every read into a miss at once.
variants.hint: Which key component describes the shape of the value?
variants.explanation: Include a representation version in the key. Old copies expire naturally instead of being flushed together.

variants.title: Choose the invalidation rule
variants.context: Every cached value must be disposable. TTL suits bounded staleness; delete-after-commit races with refills; versioned keys retire old representations; CAS rejects a write when the item changed since it was read.
variants.prompt: Two clients read a cached counter, both increment it locally, and both write back. What prevents the second write from overwriting the first?
options: Give the counter key a much longer TTL.
Use gets for a CAS token, then cas to store.
Have both clients set the new value directly.
optionFeedback: TTL is about freshness, not about concurrent updates to one item.
CAS rejects a write when another caller changed the item after it was read.
set writes regardless of prior state, so the second one wins blindly.
variants.hint: Which command can detect an intervening update?
variants.explanation: gets returns a CAS token; cas stores only if the token still matches, so a stale write is refused instead of clobbering.

variants.title: Size the source for misses
variants.context: Hit rate changes latency and source load, never correctness. Misses per second equal total reads multiplied by the miss rate, and every miss reaches the source.
variants.prompt: The cache serves 12,000 reads per second at a 95% hit rate. How many reads per second reach the source?
variants.explanation: 12,000 × 0.05 = 600 reads per second reach the source. The source must sustain that plus a cold-start surge.

mistakes.feedback: That is the hit count. Misses are the reads that reach the source.

variants.title: Size the source for misses
variants.context: Hit rate changes latency and source load, never correctness. Misses per second equal total reads multiplied by the miss rate, and every miss reaches the source.
variants.prompt: The cache pool restarts cold. Reads are 12,000 per second and the database sustains 2,000 reads per second. Without admission control, how many reads per second exceed the database’s limit?
variants.hint: During warm-up the hit rate is near zero, so every read is a miss.
variants.explanation: 12,000 misses per second against a 2,000 limit leaves 10,000 over the line. Admission control or a degraded mode must absorb them.

mistakes.feedback: That is the steady-state miss rate; a cold cache misses almost everything.
The database can take 2,000 of them; the excess is 10,000.

variants.title: Size the source for misses
variants.context: Hit rate changes latency and source load, never correctness. Misses per second equal total reads multiplied by the miss rate, and every miss reaches the source.
variants.prompt: Reads are 20,000 per second. The source can sustain 2,400 reads per second. What is the minimum hit rate, in percent, that keeps the source within its limit?
variants.hint: Misses must be at most 2,400 of 20,000.
variants.explanation: 2,400 ÷ 20,000 = 12% misses, so the hit rate must be at least 88%. Popularity, not memory coverage, decides whether that holds.

mistakes.feedback: 12% is the maximum miss rate; the question asks for the hit rate.
90% would work, but the minimum that fits is 88%.

variants.title: Design the key contract
variants.context: A cache key is a compatibility boundary. Build it in a fixed order: namespace the owner, include the representation version, choose freshness, then bound refill ownership.
variants.prompt: A catalog team designs keys for product records. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Derive the TTL from acceptable staleness and decide when to invalidate.
Namespace the owner, such as catalog:product.
Include the representation version, such as v3.
Choose single-flight, a lease, early recache, or stale serving for hot refills.

variants.hint: Collision control comes before anything about freshness.
variants.explanation: Namespace → version → freshness → refill ownership. Each step protects a different failure: collisions, schema change, staleness, and refill storms.

variants.title: Design the key contract
variants.context: A cache key is a compatibility boundary. Build it in a fixed order: namespace the owner, include the representation version, choose freshness, then bound refill ownership.
variants.prompt: A hot key expires every minute and thousands of requests hit the source together. Put the full key contract in order, ending with the fix.

items.text: Elect a single refill owner so one caller rebuilds while others wait or serve stale.
Start the key with the service and entity name.
Set the TTL with jitter so related keys do not expire on the same second.
Add a version for the serialized shape.

variants.hint: The stampede is solved by the last step, but the earlier steps still come first.
variants.explanation: The refill-ownership step is what stops the stampede: single-flight or the meta protocol’s recache ownership limits source work to one rebuild.

variants.title: Design the key contract
variants.context: A cache key is a compatibility boundary. Build it in a fixed order: namespace the owner, include the representation version, choose freshness, then bound refill ownership.
variants.prompt: Two teams accidentally share keys. Put the contract steps in order so the collision cannot recur.

items.text: Bound who may refill a popular key.
Version the representation.
Pick TTL and invalidation from the data contract.
Prefix keys with the owning service and entity.

variants.hint: The collision is fixed by the first step.
variants.explanation: Namespacing the owner prevents unrelated teams from reusing a key space; the remaining steps complete the contract.
